name: Main Course
description: The fundamentals: knife, heat, seasoning and doneness.

skills.name: Steady board
skills.description: Set up a station that doesn't slip or get in the way.

skills.name: Never cross raw
skills.description: Keep raw meat and fish away from what's eaten uncooked.

skills.name: The blunt knife is the dangerous one
skills.description: Understand why a dull blade slips and cuts you.

skills.name: Grease fires
skills.description: Smother it instead of dousing it with water, and kill the heat.

skills.name: Pinch grip
skills.description: Hold the knife by the blade with thumb and index finger, not by the handle.

skills.name: Claw hand
skills.description: Tuck your fingertips in and guide the blade with your knuckles.

skills.name: Even dice
skills.description: Cut to the same size so everything cooks at the same time.

skills.name: Mise en place
skills.description: Everything chopped and within reach before the hob goes on.

skills.name: Preheating
skills.description: Wait for the pan to be hot before anything goes in.

skills.name: Reading the heat
skills.description: Tell low, medium and high apart by sound and smell.

skills.name: Choosing the fat
skills.description: Olive oil, butter or neutral oil, by the heat each one takes.

skills.name: Browning
skills.description: Recognise a golden crust and what stops one forming.

skills.name: Low heat
skills.description: Cook slowly without burning the edges.

skills.name: Egg doneness
skills.description: Know when the white is set and the yolk still soft.

skills.name: When to salt
skills.description: When the salt goes in changes texture, not just flavour.

skills.name: Salted water
skills.description: Season from the inside, in the cooking water.

skills.name: Al dente
skills.description: Taste instead of trusting the clock.

skills.name: Water ratio
skills.description: The proportion that makes rice loose instead of mush.

skills.name: Sequencing
skills.description: Start with what takes longest so everything reaches the table hot.

skills.name: Seasoning in layers
skills.description: Salt at every stage instead of all of it at the end.

skills.name: Plating
skills.description: Hot plate, height, and a colour that contrasts.

missions.title: Your first egg
missions.summary: Ten minutes, with what you already have at home. It fails in ways you can see and fix.

steps.title: Mise en place
steps.description: Egg, salt and oil to hand, on your free hand's side. Lid within reach. Only then do you light the hob.

rescues.answer: No oil? Butter works and browns the white better — but it burns faster, so drop the heat a notch.
You're ready when you don't have to turn your back on the pan to fetch anything.

steps.title: Heat the pan
steps.description: Medium heat, empty pan, 1 to 2 minutes. A drop of water has to sizzle and vanish in seconds.

rescues.answer: The drop of water sizzles and disappears: it's ready. If it just simmers slowly, the pan is still cold.
If the pan starts smoking before the oil goes in, it's too hot. Take it off the heat for 30 seconds and put it back.

steps.title: The oil
steps.description: A drizzle of oil covering the base. Swirl the pan. The oil should run thin, not pool.

rescues.answer: Smoking oil has already lost its flavour and will make the egg bitter. Throw it out, wipe with paper and start again — 30 seconds that saves the dish.
Too little oil sticks. If the base isn't glistening all over, add another drizzle.

steps.title: Crack the egg
steps.description: Crack the egg into a bowl first, then tip it into the pan. Bring the bowl close to the base: the higher you go, the more likely the yolk breaks.

rescues.answer: Broken yolk? Not fatal — it becomes a broken-yolk fried egg and cooks just the same. Next one, crack it closer to the base.
If the white grabbed the base immediately, the pan was too hot. Lower the heat and don't try to lift it yet.

steps.title: Cook it covered
steps.description: Drop to low heat and cover. The lid cooks the surface of the white without flipping the egg. 2 to 3 minutes.

rescues.answer: The white is opaque right up to the yolk, and the yolk still wobbles when you shake the pan. That's the point.
Brown, lacy edges: too much heat. Next time, lower it the moment the egg goes in.
Don't force the spatula. Cover it for another 30 seconds: the white finishes setting and releases by itself.

steps.title: Plate it
steps.description: Spatula underneath, one movement, plate already waiting. Salt on top and now — not before, or the white releases water.

rescues.answer: If the yolk runs when you break it, you nailed it.
No spatula? Tilt the pan over the plate and let the egg slide out.

missions.title: Golden onion
missions.summary: One onion, one pan and patience: the base of half of what you are going to cook.

steps.title: Chop
steps.description: Onion halved, root whole, grid of cuts and then slice across. 5 mm dice, all the same.

rescues.answer: Uneven dice give you burnt pieces and raw pieces in the same pan. It's worth going back over the big ones.
If you can stack two cubes and they look the same size, that's good enough.

steps.title: Heat with fat
steps.description: Medium heat, oil covering the base, and only then the onion. It has to sizzle as it goes in.

rescues.answer: Sizzles as it goes in: you're there. If it's silent, take the onion out and heat the pan more.
Oil smoking before the onion goes in: start again, it's already burnt.

steps.title: Sweat
steps.description: Stir now and then. The onion turns translucent before it takes on colour. 8 to 10 minutes.

rescues.answer: A base that's catching means too much heat. Lower it and add a spoon of water — the steam lifts what stuck and it goes into the flavour.
Black edges burn bitter and don't come back. Lower the heat and stir more often.

steps.title: Brown it
steps.description: Now for colour. Stir less and let it go golden brown, not dark brown.

rescues.answer: Honey colour, a sweet smell, and the onion has shrunk by half. That's it.
Scrape the base with the wooden spoon: that's flavour, not dirt.

missions.title: An omelette that doesn't burn
missions.summary: The low-heat test: if the base went brown, the heat was too high.

steps.title: Beat
steps.description: Eggs beaten until white and yolk are one colour. Salt now.

rescues.answer: An even colour, no streaks of white showing.
No whisk? A fork and twenty seconds will do.

steps.title: Low heat
steps.description: Butter melting without foaming much. Low heat — this is where almost everyone goes wrong.

rescues.answer: Brown butter: the heat is too high. Wipe it out and start again, the omelette would taste burnt.
The butter spreads and foams finely, without darkening.

steps.title: Cook it slowly
steps.description: Eggs in, then keep pulling the edges into the centre with a spatula, tilting the pan.

rescues.answer: Sticking in a non-stick pan means too much heat. Take it off for 20 seconds.
Base set, surface still slightly moist. That's when you fold.

steps.title: Fold and serve
steps.description: Fold it in half, give it 20 seconds and slide it onto the plate. The base must have no colour.

rescues.answer: A brown base is the classic mistake: too much heat. A French omelette is pale on purpose.
If it tore as you folded, it needed longer. Give it another 20 seconds before moving it.

missions.title: Loose rice
missions.summary: Measuring instead of guessing. It is the ratio that decides, not talent.

steps.title: Measure
steps.description: One measure of rice to two of water. Measure it — this isn't for guessing.

rescues.answer: No measuring cup? Use any glass: what counts is the ratio, not the size.
Two to one. That number decides whether it's loose or mush.

steps.title: Toast the rice
steps.description: Oil, dry rice, stir for 1 minute until the grains glisten.

rescues.answer: Keep stirring: dry rice catches quickly.
Glistening grains, translucent at the tips.

steps.title: Water and salt
steps.description: Add the boiling water and the salt. Bring it back to the boil, cover and drop to the lowest heat.

rescues.answer: Cold water holds everything up and the rice absorbs badly. Boil it first.
As soon as it boils, cover and drop the heat. From here the lid stays on.

steps.title: Don't stir
steps.description: 12 minutes covered, without lifting the lid. Stirring breaks the grains and releases starch: that's what makes mush.

rescues.answer: After 12 minutes turn it off and leave it covered for 5 before opening.
A burnt smell means too much heat: turn it off, don't scrape the base, and serve only from the top.

missions.title: A whole dish
missions.summary: Three things at once, everything hot at the table. This is where the difference shows.

steps.title: Sequence it
steps.description: The rice takes 20 minutes, the chicken 25, the salad 5. Start with the chicken.

rescues.answer: Write the order down before you light anything: chicken, rice, salad.
If something is done and the rest isn't, cover it and set it aside — warm beats raw.

steps.title: Chicken
steps.description: Season it and put it on medium-high heat, skin down, without moving it for 6 minutes.

rescues.answer: It's sticking because it hasn't formed a crust yet. Once it's golden it releases by itself.
Deep golden skin and no pink near the bone.

steps.title: Rice in parallel
steps.description: With the chicken cooking, make the rice. Two to one, covered, 12 minutes.

rescues.answer: Two hobs at once means lowering both. Better slow than burnt.

steps.title: Season in layers
steps.description: Salt on the chicken beforehand, salt in the rice water, salt and lemon on the salad at the end.

rescues.answer: If it tastes flat, everything was seasoned at the end. Salt at each stage tastes different from salt on top.

steps.title: Plate it
steps.description: Warm plate, rice as the base, chicken on top, salad alongside. A colour that contrasts.

rescues.answer: If all three reached the table hot at the same time, you sequenced it well.

lessons.title: The board that won't betray you
lessons.description: Before any cut: where you put the board decides whether you cut yourself.

preparationSteps.title: Clean and dry
preparationSteps.description: Empty, dry counter. A wet counter makes the board slide.

preparationSteps.title: Lock the board down
preparationSteps.description: A damp cloth folded under the board. Push it: it mustn't move.

preparationSteps.title: Make room
preparationSteps.description: Clear everything you don't need within arm's reach.

preparationSteps.title: A board for raw
preparationSteps.description: If you're handling raw meat or fish, set the second board aside now.

tips.title: Room around the board
tips.text: Leave about 20 cm free on each side: enough for a bowl of what you've cut and somewhere to rest the knife.

questions.prompt: The board slides on the counter every time you cut. What do you do?
options: Put a folded damp cloth underneath
Hold the board with my free hand
Cut more slowly
Push the board against the wall
questions.correctAnswer: Put a folded damp cloth underneath
questions.explanation: A damp cloth grips on both sides and costs nothing. It's the first move in any professional kitchen.
questions.explainWrong: Holding the board with your free hand puts that hand exactly where the knife is going. It's the wrong trade: you fix the sliding by creating a target.

questions.prompt: You've just cut raw chicken. Next you need to cut lettuce. What do you do with the board?
options: Wash it with hot water and soap, or use another board
Rinse it under cold water
Wipe it with kitchen paper
Flip the board over
questions.correctAnswer: Wash it with hot water and soap, or use another board
questions.explanation: The lettuce never goes back on the heat. Anything left from the chicken goes straight to the plate.
questions.explainWrong: Flipping the board or wiping it with paper spreads instead of removing — and salad is precisely what isn't going to be cooked afterwards.

questions.prompt: Put in order what you do before the first cut.
correctOrder: Wash your hands
Wipe and dry the counter
Put the damp cloth under the board
Put the knife and ingredients within reach
questions.explanation: The order isn't arbitrary: each step only makes sense once the one before it is done.
questions.explainWrong: Putting the board down before drying the counter means lifting everything again. And the knife is always the last thing onto the counter — before that you have nowhere safe to rest it.

questions.prompt: Is this counter ready to start cutting?
options: Yes, it's workable
No, there's no free space around the board
questions.correctAnswer: No, there's no free space around the board
questions.explanation: You need room for what you've already cut. Without it, the cuts pile up on the board and the next one gets cramped.
questions.explainWrong: A full counter looks productive but forces you to cut inside a small square. That's where the knife meets a jar instead of the board.

questions.prompt: You're going to the fridge for an ingredient. Where do you put the knife?
options: On the counter, edge facing in and handle away from the edge
In the sink
On the board, handle hanging off
In the bowl of chopped ingredients
questions.correctAnswer: On the counter, edge facing in and handle away from the edge
questions.explanation: The knife has to be visible and away from the edge. It's the only position where nobody touches it by accident.
questions.explainWrong: In the sink the knife disappears under the foam and cuts whoever washes up. A handle hanging off the board is what makes it fall — and a falling knife is never caught.

lessons.title: The blunt knife is the one that cuts you
lessons.description: The blade that won't cut a tomato is the one that cuts you. Here's why.

preparationSteps.title: The tomato test
preparationSteps.description: Rest the blade on the tomato's skin and draw it back without pressing.

preparationSteps.title: Read the result
preparationSteps.description: If the skin gives, you have an edge. If the blade slides, you don't.

preparationSteps.title: If it didn't cut
preparationSteps.description: The knife needs sharpening. Take it to be sharpened or ask someone who knows. Until then, use another knife that passes the test.

preparationSteps.title: Test it again
preparationSteps.description: Once sharpened, go back to the tomato. It has to bite first time.

tips.title: Test before you sharpen
tips.text: If the knife bites the tomato first time, it needs nothing. Sharpening is only worth it once the blade slides.

tips.title: Sharpening, if you want to go further
tips.text: On a steel, the blade goes at about 20°. If you're not comfortable with it, no problem: have the knife sharpened and use the tomato test to know when.

questions.prompt: Why is a blunt knife more dangerous than a sharp one?
options: It slides instead of biting, and your hand follows
It heats up faster
It forces you to cut more slowly
It rusts more easily
questions.correctAnswer: It slides instead of biting, and your hand follows
questions.explanation: A sharp blade goes in where you put it. A blunt one skates across the surface and ends up where you weren't expecting — usually the hand holding things.
questions.explainWrong: The danger isn't the knife cutting well. It's the knife not cutting and you making up for it with force: more force on a blade that slides is exactly the recipe for an accident.

questions.prompt: The blade slid across the tomato's skin without marking it. Is this knife ready to use?
options: Yes, just press harder
No, it needs an edge before it cuts
questions.correctAnswer: No, it needs an edge before it cuts
questions.explanation: The tomato test is binary: either the skin gives to the weight of the blade, or you have no edge.
questions.explainWrong: "Press harder" is the answer that sends people to A&E. If the blade won't bite under its own weight, what force changes is how fast it slides.

questions.prompt: The knife slips off the counter and is falling. What do you do?
options: Step back and let it fall
Catch it by the handle
Try to push it back onto the counter
Put my foot underneath
questions.correctAnswer: Step back and let it fall
questions.explanation: A falling knife spins. There's no telling which part reaches your hand first.
questions.explainWrong: Catching it by the handle works in films because the handle is always facing up. In a real kitchen the knife turns, and your hand meets the edge mid-spin.

questions.prompt: How do you wash the knife after using it?
options: By hand, straight away, and dry it
In the dishwasher with everything else
Leave it to soak until after dinner
Rinse it and put it away wet
questions.correctAnswer: By hand, straight away, and dry it
questions.explanation: The dishwasher knocks the blade against everything else and eats the edge. Standing water eats the steel.
questions.explainWrong: Leaving it to soak combines both problems: the knife disappears into water someone will reach into, and the edge spends an hour oxidising.

lessons.title: Holding the knife
lessons.description: Nobody taught you how to hold a knife. That's why you're tired after two onions.

preparationSteps.title: Move your hand up
preparationSteps.description: Thumb and index finger grip the blade, just in front of the handle.

preparationSteps.title: Close the rest
preparationSteps.description: The other three fingers wrap around the handle.

preparationSteps.title: Test the balance
preparationSteps.description: The knife should balance by itself between your fingers.

preparationSteps.title: Cut without the wrist
preparationSteps.description: The movement comes from the shoulder and elbow, not the wrist.

tips.title: The tip barely leaves the board
tips.text: Cutting is pushing forward and down, not chopping. The tip stays about 3 cm off the board.

questions.prompt: Where do the thumb and index finger go in the pinch grip?
options: Gripping the blade, in front of the handle
Stretched along the top of the handle
Both wrapped around the handle
Thumb on top of the edge
questions.correctAnswer: Gripping the blade, in front of the handle
questions.explanation: Holding the blade puts your hand at the knife's centre of gravity. You go from holding it to steering it.
questions.explainWrong: With every finger on the handle, the knife becomes a lever and the wrist does all the work — it's why you get tired and the cut goes crooked halfway through an onion.

questions.prompt: Your wrist hurts after two carrots. What's wrong?
options: I'm cutting with my wrist instead of my arm
The knife is too light
The board is too high
I'm cutting too slowly
questions.correctAnswer: I'm cutting with my wrist instead of my arm
questions.explanation: The cut comes from the shoulder, with the wrist fixed. The wrist only steers.
questions.explainWrong: If the pain is in your wrist, the joint doing the work is the weakest in the chain. Changing knives doesn't fix a problem that's about movement.

questions.prompt: Put the steps for picking up the knife in order.
correctOrder: Rest the knife on the board, edge down
Pinch the blade with thumb and index finger
Close the other three fingers around the handle
Lift it and check it balances on its own
questions.explanation: Always gripping from the board avoids adjusting with the knife in the air.
questions.explainWrong: Adjusting your grip with the knife already lifted is the moment the blade turns inwards. Every adjustment is made with the knife resting down.

questions.prompt: The hand in this picture holds the whole handle, index finger stretched along the spine of the blade. Is it correct?
options: Yes, that's the right grip
No, the stretched finger costs you control
questions.correctAnswer: No, the stretched finger costs you control
questions.explanation: The index finger stretched on top looks like it gives direction, but it takes away power and knocks the blade out of line on long cuts.
questions.explainWrong: It's the most common grip among self-taught cooks, and also the one that lets the blade wander sideways by the third cut — a stretched finger doesn't stop the knife rotating.

questions.prompt: You need to pass the knife to someone else. How?
options: Put it on the counter and let them pick it up
Hand it over by the handle, edge down
Hand it over by the blade
Toss it onto the counter beside them
questions.correctAnswer: Put it on the counter and let them pick it up
questions.explanation: Never two hands on the same knife at once. The counter is the middleman.
questions.explainWrong: Handing it over by the handle seems polite, but it makes two people hold the knife at the same time — and whoever hands it over always lets go before the other has a proper grip.

lessons.title: The claw hand
lessons.description: The hand that isn't holding the knife is the one that gets cut. There's a way to put it out of reach.

preparationSteps.title: Tuck the tips in
preparationSteps.description: Curl your fingers as if you were holding a small ball.

preparationSteps.title: Rest the blade
preparationSteps.description: The side of the blade rests against your knuckles.

preparationSteps.title: Steer with the knuckles
preparationSteps.description: The knuckles are the stop. The blade never gets past them.

preparationSteps.title: Walk the hand back
preparationSteps.description: With each cut, the hand moves back by the width of the next slice.

tips.title: Your hand sets the thickness
tips.text: How far the hand moves back between cuts is the thickness of the slice. For thin slices, about 5 mm at a time.

questions.prompt: What acts as the stop for the blade in the claw grip?
options: Your knuckles
Your nails
Your thumb
Your palm
questions.correctAnswer: Your knuckles
questions.explanation: The knuckles are the most prominent part of a curled hand. The blade rests against them and never reaches your fingertips.
questions.explainWrong: Nails and fingertips are exactly what the claw hides. If the blade touches them, the hand isn't curled enough.

questions.prompt: Put the cycle of a claw-hand cut in order.
correctOrder: Curl your fingers and hold the ingredient
Rest the side of the blade against your knuckles
Cut, letting the blade slide along your knuckles
Move your hand back by the thickness of the next slice
questions.explanation: Every cut closes the cycle in the same place: that's what makes it repeatable and safe.
questions.explainWrong: Moving your hand back before cutting removes the blade's stop at the exact moment it comes down. The hand only moves back once the knife has passed.

questions.prompt: In this picture the fingers are stretched out holding the carrot. Can you cut like that?
options: Yes, as long as I cut slowly
No, the fingertips are in the way
questions.correctAnswer: No, the fingertips are in the way
questions.explanation: With fingers stretched out there's no stop. The only thing between the blade and your nail is your attention.
questions.explainWrong: "Slowly" isn't protection — it's what you do while you're concentrating, and nobody concentrates through a whole onion. The claw protects you even when you drift off.

questions.prompt: You're cutting a round courgette that rolls on the board. What do you do first?
options: Cut a thin slice lengthways to make a flat base
Hold it tighter
Cut it straight down the middle while it rolls
Use a bigger knife
questions.correctAnswer: Cut a thin slice lengthways to make a flat base
questions.explanation: Nothing round is cut safely. The first job is giving it a flat face to sit on.
questions.explainWrong: Holding a rolling object tighter just moves the problem to your fingers. Whatever rolls has to stop rolling before the knife goes in.

questions.prompt: Halfway through an onion you catch your fingers stretched out again. Why?
options: The claw is tiring until it becomes habit — it's normal, and you fix it by pausing
The knife isn't sharp enough
The board is too small
I'm cutting too fast
questions.correctAnswer: The claw is tiring until it becomes habit — it's normal, and you fix it by pausing
questions.explanation: In the first few weeks the hand undoes the claw on its own. Noticing and curling it back is the training.
questions.explainWrong: Blaming the knife or the board puts off what matters: the claw is a new movement, and new movements fall apart under fatigue. The fix is a two-second pause, not new kit.

lessons.title: Diced onion
lessons.description: The cut that shows up in half the recipes you're going to make.

preparationSteps.title: Halve it
preparationSteps.description: Top to root. The root stays whole in both halves.

preparationSteps.title: Peel it
preparationSteps.description: Take the skin off, leaving the root. That's what holds everything together.

preparationSteps.title: Horizontal cuts
preparationSteps.description: Two or three cuts parallel to the board, stopping short of the root.

preparationSteps.title: Vertical cuts
preparationSteps.description: Cuts from top to bottom, again without cutting the root.

preparationSteps.title: Slice across
preparationSteps.description: Now cut the other way: the dice fall out by themselves.

tips.title: Small dice for a soffritto
tips.text: Dice of about 5 mm soften in a few minutes without disappearing into the sauce.

tips.title: On the flat cuts, your hand goes on top
tips.text: When you cut the onion horizontally, lay your palm flat on top of it. It's the one time you don't use the claw.

questions.prompt: Why do you leave the onion's root whole?
options: It's what holds all the layers together
It has more flavour
It's the part you eat
It stops you crying
questions.correctAnswer: It's what holds all the layers together
questions.explanation: Without the root, the onion falls apart into loose layers at the first cut and there's nothing left to cut.
questions.explainWrong: The root isn't about flavour or tears — it's structural. Cutting it off first turns the onion into a pile of layers that run from under the knife.

questions.prompt: Put the onion dice in order.
correctOrder: Halve it from top to root
Peel it, leaving the root on
Make the horizontal cuts, stopping short of the root
Make the vertical cuts, stopping short of the root
Slice across to release the dice
questions.explanation: The three sets of cuts make a grid. The last cut is the only one that releases anything.
questions.explainWrong: Slicing before making the grid gives you half-moons, not dice. And peeling before halving leaves you spinning a slippery sphere on the board.

questions.prompt: This chopped onion has pieces the size of a pea and others the size of a fingernail. Is it good enough for a soffritto?
options: Yes, it all breaks down anyway
No, the small ones burn before the big ones cook
questions.correctAnswer: No, the small ones burn before the big ones cook
questions.explanation: Even sizing isn't about looks: it's what makes everything finish at the same time.
questions.explainWrong: It doesn't all break down evenly. The small pieces turn bitter while the big ones are still raw, and that bitterness goes into the whole sauce.

questions.prompt: The tears are stopping you seeing what you're cutting. What actually helps?
options: A cold onion and a sharp knife
Holding your breath
Cutting under running water
Holding a spoon in your mouth
questions.correctAnswer: A cold onion and a sharp knife
questions.explanation: What makes you cry is the gas released by ruptured cells. Cold slows the reaction, and a clean cut ruptures fewer cells.
questions.explainWrong: The spoon and breath-holding tricks don't touch the cause. If the blade crushes instead of cutting, it ruptures more cells and releases more gas — a blunt knife literally makes you cry.

lessons.title: Everything ready before the heat
lessons.description: The rule that separates cooking from chasing the hob: nothing heats up before everything is chopped.
ingredients: A lid that fits the pan

preparationSteps.title: Read the recipe to the end
preparationSteps.description: Before cutting anything at all. Half of all mistakes start here.

preparationSteps.title: Chop everything
preparationSteps.description: Each ingredient in its own bowl, in the order it goes in.

preparationSteps.title: Line them up in order
preparationSteps.description: The bowls sit to the side of the hob, in the order they're used.

preparationSteps.title: Lid and cloth within reach
preparationSteps.description: The lid is your fire extinguisher. The dry cloth is for hot handles.

preparationSteps.title: Only now light the hob
preparationSteps.description: With everything lined up, turning on the heat is the last move.

tips.title: Count on 10 minutes
tips.text: Prepping everything for a simple soffritto takes about 10 minutes. It sounds like a lot, but it saves you the scramble later.

questions.prompt: Why do you chop everything before turning on the hob?
options: Because once the heat is on, the time belongs to the food, not to you
Because it means less washing up
Because the food tastes better
Because it's faster overall
questions.correctAnswer: Because once the heat is on, the time belongs to the food, not to you
questions.explanation: With the pan hot you no longer set the pace. If you still have garlic to chop, the garlic arrives late and what's in the pan burns.
questions.explainWrong: Overall it may well take the same. What changes is where the pressure sits: chopping calmly beforehand, or chopping with the onion darkening behind you.

questions.prompt: The oil in the pan has caught fire. What do you do?
options: Turn off the heat and cover it with a lid
Throw water on it
Take the pan to the sink
Blow the flames out
questions.correctAnswer: Turn off the heat and cover it with a lid
questions.explanation: Fire needs oxygen. Covering it cuts that off. Water on burning oil turns to steam and throws flaming oil everywhere.
questions.explainWrong: Water on burning fat is the worst thing you can do: it flashes to steam instantly and throws burning oil over you and the rest of the kitchen.

questions.prompt: Put the prep before lighting the hob in order.
correctOrder: Read the recipe from start to finish
Cut everything and separate it into bowls
Line the bowls up in the order they go in
Put the lid and a dry cloth within reach
Light the hob
questions.explanation: Reading first is what stops you discovering halfway through that an ingredient was missing. Lighting the hob is always the last step.
questions.explainWrong: Chopping before reading the whole recipe is how improvising starts: at step four you find the onion was meant to be in half-moons and you've already diced it.

questions.prompt: The bowls are full and lined up, but on the right of the hob — and you're right-handed, with the spoon in your right hand. Is that fine?
options: Yes, as long as they're in order
No, the bowls go on your free hand's side
questions.correctAnswer: No, the bowls go on your free hand's side
questions.explanation: The stirring hand doesn't let go of the spoon. Ingredients go in with the other one.
questions.explainWrong: The right order on the wrong side makes you reach across a hot pan for every ingredient. That's the move that knocks bowls over and burns forearms.

questions.prompt: The recipe says the onion goes in first and the garlic two minutes later. How do you prep?
options: Separate bowls: together, the garlic burns
Same bowl, they go in almost at the same time
Chop the garlic during those two minutes
Put both in at the start and lower the heat
questions.correctAnswer: Separate bowls: together, the garlic burns
questions.explanation: Garlic takes a third of the onion's time. In the same bowl they always end up in the pan together.
questions.explainWrong: Chopping the garlic during those two minutes is exactly what mise en place exists to avoid — two minutes watching the clock is too little time to chop and too long with your back to the pan.

units.title: Unit 2
units.subtitle: Let the heat do the work

lessons.title: A cold pan sears nothing
lessons.description: Almost everything that goes wrong in a pan starts before the food goes in.

preparationSteps.title: Empty pan on the heat
preparationSteps.description: Medium heat, nothing in it. Two to three minutes.

preparationSteps.title: The water-drop test
preparationSteps.description: Drop in a few drops of water. If they dance across the pan, it's hot.

preparationSteps.title: Only now the fat
preparationSteps.description: Enough oil to cover the base. It spreads instantly when the pan is ready.

preparationSteps.title: And only then the food
preparationSteps.description: It has to sizzle as it goes in. If it goes in silently, it wasn't ready.

tips.title: Give the pan time
tips.text: On medium heat, a pan needs about 3 minutes to be ready. That's what separates browned from boiled.

questions.prompt: You put the steak in a pan that was still lukewarm. What happens?
options: It releases water and ends up boiled instead of browned
Same result, it just takes a minute longer
It burns outside and stays raw inside
It sticks less to the base
questions.correctAnswer: It releases water and ends up boiled instead of browned
questions.explanation: Without enough heat, the meat releases its own juices faster than they evaporate. It sits there swimming and stewing.
questions.explainWrong: It isn't about taking longer: something else is happening. Below a certain temperature there's no crust to form at all, just water coming out — and boiling water browns nothing.

questions.prompt: Put the start of any sauté in order.
correctOrder: Empty pan over medium heat
Wait until it is properly hot
Add the fat
Add the food — it has to sizzle
questions.explanation: The pan heats first, the fat goes in near the end. That way the fat spends little time on the heat and never burns.
questions.explainWrong: Putting the oil in a cold pan is the most common home-kitchen mistake: it sits there heating for the whole three minutes, and a fat that smokes before the food goes in is already burnt.

questions.prompt: The oil in this pan is smoking and the food hasn't gone in yet. Can you carry on?
options: Yes, the hotter the better the sear
No, that oil is already burnt
questions.correctAnswer: No, that oil is already burnt
questions.explanation: Smoke is the fat going past its limit. The bitterness that shows up there stays in everything that goes in next.
questions.explainWrong: Hotter isn't always better. Past the smoke point the fat breaks down — the bitterness won't come out of anything, and the best move is to start again with a clean pan.

questions.prompt: How do you know the pan is hot before the fat goes in?
options: A few drops of water dance on the surface instead of evaporating at once
The handle feels hot
You can see the base change colour
Exactly two minutes have passed on the clock
questions.correctAnswer: A few drops of water dance on the surface instead of evaporating at once
questions.explanation: It's called the Leidenfrost effect: the drop floats on its own vapour. It's a thermometer you already own.
questions.explainWrong: The clock knows nothing about your hob, and the handle or the base tell you nothing reliable. The drop does — and it costs nothing.

lessons.title: High, medium, low
lessons.description: Three different heats do three different things. It isn't a speed dial.

preparationSteps.title: High heat
preparationSteps.description: For searing and browning. The food sizzles loudly and you barely move it.

preparationSteps.title: Medium heat
preparationSteps.description: For sweating and frying gently. A quiet sizzle, with time to stir.

preparationSteps.title: Low heat
preparationSteps.description: For reducing. A bubble shows up now and then, no more.

preparationSteps.title: Switching mid-dish
preparationSteps.description: Sear high, finish medium: the heat isn't a single choice.

tips.title: How to recognise low heat
tips.text: In a sauce on low heat you see the odd bubble, not a constant boil.

questions.prompt: You want soft, sweet onion for a soffritto. Which heat?
options: Medium, for a good while
High, to get it over with
Low, with a lid on
High first and low straight after
questions.correctAnswer: Medium, for a good while
questions.explanation: An onion's sweetness comes out slowly. On medium it sweats, softens and sweetens without the edges ever burning.
questions.explainWrong: On high heat the edges go black before the middle softens, and the bitterness goes into the whole sauce. Sweet onion is a matter of time, not power.

questions.prompt: This pan is sizzling loudly and smoke is coming off the sides. You're sweating onion. Right or wrong?
options: Right, that's how you do it quickly
Wrong, that's searing heat, not sweating heat
questions.correctAnswer: Wrong, that's searing heat, not sweating heat
questions.explanation: Smoke and a loud sizzle are the heat that sears a steak. An onion at that heat burns outside before it sweetens inside.
questions.explainWrong: Quick isn't the goal — it's what ruins the soffritto. Drop to medium: it still sizzles, but quietly, and now you have time to stir.

questions.prompt: Put the heats for a steak with a pan sauce in order.
correctOrder: High heat to sear both sides
Take the meat out and drop to medium
Sweat the onion in what is left in the pan
Low heat to reduce the sauce
questions.explanation: The same pan does three jobs. What changes between them is the heat, and that change is what makes the dish.
questions.explainWrong: Leaving the heat high from start to finish burns the base before the sauce reduces — and what was on the base was all the steak's flavour.

questions.prompt: The food has started sticking and going too dark. What's the first move?
options: Lower the heat, and only then scrape the base with a spoon
Add more oil on top
Take the pan off the heat and let it cool right down
Turn the heat up to loosen what's stuck
questions.correctAnswer: Lower the heat, and only then scrape the base with a spoon
questions.explanation: Remove the cause first, then deal with the effect. What's stuck is flavour, as long as it isn't black.
questions.explainWrong: More oil on an overheated base just smokes more, and turning the heat up speeds along what was already going wrong. The cause is too much heat — that's what you fix first.

lessons.title: Every fat takes its own heat
lessons.description: Extra virgin olive oil in a screaming wok is money thrown away and free bitterness.

preparationSteps.title: Smoke point
preparationSteps.description: The temperature at which a fat breaks down and turns bitter.

preparationSteps.title: Extra virgin olive oil
preparationSteps.description: Real flavour, low smoke point. Best raw or on medium heat.

preparationSteps.title: Neutral oil
preparationSteps.description: Little flavour, takes high heat. This is the one for frying and searing.

preparationSteps.title: Butter
preparationSteps.description: Burns quickly because of the milk solids. Add it at the end, or with a little oil.

tips.title: A little fat is enough
tips.text: To sauté, a thin film covering the base of the pan is enough. More than that is frying.

questions.prompt: You're searing a steak on high heat. Which fat?
options: Neutral oil, and butter only at the end
Extra virgin olive oil, it has more flavour
Butter from the start, for better browning
None: a non-stick pan doesn't need it
questions.correctAnswer: Neutral oil, and butter only at the end
questions.explanation: The oil takes searing temperature; the butter goes in for the last seconds, for flavour without burning.
questions.explainWrong: Butter contains milk solids, and they burn well below searing temperature — black in the pan and bitter on the steak. Extra virgin olive oil, at that heat, loses exactly what makes it expensive.

questions.prompt: The butter in this pan has dark brown specks and smells strongly toasted. Good for finishing the sauce?
options: Yes, that's beurre noisette and it adds flavour
No, this is past noisette and it's burnt
questions.correctAnswer: No, this is past noisette and it's burnt
questions.explanation: Beurre noisette is golden and smells of nuts. Black specks and a harsh smell are the next stage, and there's no going back.
questions.explainWrong: There is a window where browned butter is superb — but it's short, and what closes it is the dark colour and the burnt smell. Past that window, the bitterness stays.

questions.prompt: Put a seared steak finished in butter in order.
correctOrder: Pan properly hot
Neutral oil, just covering the base
Sear the meat on both sides
Lower the heat and add the butter
Baste the meat with the butter from the pan
questions.explanation: The oil does the hard work, the butter does the flavour. Each goes in at the temperature it can take.
questions.explainWrong: Butter at the start, with the pan at searing heat, turns black before the meat gets a crust — and from there the dish is bitter.

questions.prompt: A pan of oil has caught fire. What do you do?
options: Turn off the heat and cover it with a lid
Throw water on it, fast
Carry the pan to the sink
Blow hard to put it out
questions.correctAnswer: Turn off the heat and cover it with a lid
questions.explanation: With no oxygen, the fire goes out. Lid on and heat off settles it in seconds.
questions.explainWrong: Water on burning oil flashes to steam and throws flaming oil over you and the kitchen. And walking with a burning pan spreads the fire along the way.

lessons.title: Golden brown, not dark brown
lessons.description: Colour isn't decoration: it's flavour that doesn't exist until it appears.

preparationSteps.title: Spread it out
preparationSteps.description: Piled-up food releases steam and stews. One layer, with space.

preparationSteps.title: Don't stir constantly
preparationSteps.description: Colour needs contact with the base. Stirring every thirty seconds is plenty.

preparationSteps.title: Follow the smell
preparationSteps.description: The smell changes before the colour. Sweet is a good sign; sharp is a warning.

preparationSteps.title: Stop in time
preparationSteps.description: Honey-coloured is the target. Honey to black takes less than a minute.

questions.prompt: You put all the mushrooms in at once and they released water instead of browning. Why?
options: The pan was crowded and the temperature dropped off a cliff
The mushrooms were old
There wasn't enough salt
There wasn't enough fat
questions.correctAnswer: The pan was crowded and the temperature dropped off a cliff
questions.explanation: Too much cold food at once steals the pan's heat. With no temperature there's no browning, only steam.
questions.explainWrong: It isn't the mushrooms or the salt: it's physics. A crowded pan takes time to get its heat back, and while it doesn't, it's stewing what's in it.

questions.prompt: This onion is honey-coloured, has shrunk by half and smells sweet. Take it out or leave it longer?
options: Take it out: this is the point
Leave it five more minutes, the darker the better
questions.correctAnswer: Take it out: this is the point
questions.explanation: Honey colour, half the volume and a sweet smell are the three signs together. It's peak flavour, right before the bitterness starts.
questions.explainWrong: Darker isn't more flavour — from here the colour comes from what's burning, and the sweetness that took ten minutes to appear disappears in one.

questions.prompt: How long does diced onion take to go golden on medium heat?
questions.explanation: About twelve minutes. Anyone who says three is talking about onion that's merely translucent, which is something else.
questions.explainWrong: In two minutes the onion hasn't even sweated, and half an hour on medium takes it from golden to dry. The time really is this, and there's no shortcut.

questions.prompt: Put what the onion does, from start to finish, in order.
correctOrder: It sizzles as it hits the hot fat
It turns translucent and loses the white
It shrinks and starts to colour at the edges
It turns honey-coloured and smells sweet
questions.explanation: There are four distinct stages. Knowing which one you're in is knowing how long is left.
questions.explainWrong: Colour never comes before the onion turns translucent. If brown shows up right at the start, that isn't browning — it's too much heat burning the edges.

questions.prompt: What's a pinch of salt on the onion at the very start for?
options: It draws the water out and the onion softens faster
Just seasoning, it makes no difference when it goes in
It stops the onion taking on colour
It makes the onion crisp
questions.correctAnswer: It draws the water out and the onion softens faster
questions.explanation: Salt pulls water out by osmosis. With less water inside, the onion sweats faster and reaches the colour stage sooner.
questions.explainWrong: When you salt isn't neutral: here salt is a tool, not just seasoning. And it stops no colour at all — it gets you there sooner.

lessons.title: Slow is a technique too
lessons.description: Some things only happen on low heat, and none of them happen faster if you turn it up.

preparationSteps.title: Recognise it
preparationSteps.description: Rare bubbles rising slowly. No churning surface.

preparationSteps.title: What it's for
preparationSteps.description: Reducing sauces, cooking scrambled eggs, melting without splitting.

preparationSteps.title: Adjust
preparationSteps.description: If it's properly boiling, lower it. If it stops bubbling, nudge it up.

preparationSteps.title: Be patient
preparationSteps.description: Low heat can't be rushed. Turning it up is changing technique, not going faster.

tips.title: A simmer is below the boil
tips.text: A simmer sits around 90 °C: the sauce moves gently, but it doesn't boil.

questions.prompt: Why is a tomato sauce better simmered than boiled?
options: Boiling churns and breaks everything up; a simmer lets the flavours come together
A simmer cooks faster
It's only to use less gas
Boiling makes tomato more acidic
questions.correctAnswer: Boiling churns and breaks everything up; a simmer lets the flavours come together
questions.explanation: Boiling stirs the sauce constantly and breaks up what should stay whole. On a simmer the water leaves slowly and the flavour concentrates without violence.
questions.explainWrong: Faster is exactly the opposite: a simmer takes longer on purpose. Time on the heat is part of the recipe, not a cost to cut.

questions.prompt: This pan's surface is churning with bubbles everywhere. Would you call that a simmer?
options: Yes, the bubbles are small
No, that's a boil — a simmer is the occasional bubble
questions.correctAnswer: No, that's a boil — a simmer is the occasional bubble
questions.explanation: On a simmer the surface barely moves. A bubble here, another there, and nothing more.
questions.explainWrong: Bubble size is misleading; what counts is the surface. If it's churning, the sauce is being beaten while it reduces — and what should turn creamy falls apart.

questions.prompt: Put reducing a sauce in order.
correctOrder: Bring it to the boil over medium heat
Drop it until the bubbles are rare
Let it reduce uncovered
Taste and adjust right at the end
questions.explanation: You bring it to the boil to reach temperature quickly, then drop it straight down. Covered, the water can't leave and the sauce won't reduce.
questions.explainWrong: Tasting and seasoning at the start is betting blind: as water leaves, the salt already in there concentrates — what was right at the beginning is salty at the end.

questions.prompt: The sauce is catching on the base even on low heat. What's most likely?
options: The pan is thin and makes a hot spot where the sauce burns
The heat is still too high, there's nothing else to consider
It needs salt
The sauce has too much water
questions.correctAnswer: The pan is thin and makes a hot spot where the sauce burns
questions.explanation: A thin base heats in spots instead of evenly. Stirring and scraping the base often fixes it; a heavy-based pan fixes it better.
questions.explainWrong: Not everything is the heat. With the heat already low and the sauce still catching, the problem is the pan — and going lower still just stops it reducing.

lessons.title: An egg cooks on the heat it already has
lessons.description: The commonest mistake with eggs is taking them off the heat when they're done — instead of a little before.

preparationSteps.title: Beat, but not too much
preparationSteps.description: Until yolk and white come together. Too much foam gives a dry omelette.

preparationSteps.title: Low heat from the start
preparationSteps.description: Eggs don't need high heat and don't like it.

preparationSteps.title: Stir slowly
preparationSteps.description: Push what's set from the base into the middle and let the liquid run into its place.

preparationSteps.title: Take them off early
preparationSteps.description: Take them out while the egg still glistens. The plate's heat finishes the job.

tips.title: Eggs don't need high heat
tips.text: The white starts setting just above 60 °C, long before water boils. High heat leaves it rubbery.

questions.prompt: Why do scrambled eggs turn out dry even when you take them off at the right moment?
options: They keep cooking on the plate from the heat they already hold
There wasn't enough butter
They weren't beaten enough
The eggs were cold from the fridge
questions.correctAnswer: They keep cooking on the plate from the heat they already hold
questions.explanation: It's called carryover cooking. Between pan and table the egg moves on a stage — which is why you take it off early.
questions.explainWrong: Butter helps, but it doesn't stop physics: eggs that leave the pan perfect arrive at the table dry. The fix isn't cooking better, it's stopping sooner.

questions.prompt: These scrambled eggs are dry, broken into firm curds and catching on the pan. Did they come off the heat at the right moment?
options: No, they were already past it before they left the heat
Yes, that is what cooked scrambled eggs look like
questions.correctAnswer: No, they were already past it before they left the heat
questions.explanation: An egg carries on cooking in its own heat after the pan. Wait until it looks done in the pan and it reaches the plate dry — it has to come off while still glistening and a little loose.
questions.explainWrong: That look belongs on the plate, not in the pan. By the time eggs set this firmly over the heat, the residual heat has already taken them one step further.

questions.prompt: Put creamy scrambled eggs in order.
correctOrder: Beat the eggs only until they are even
Butter in a pan over low heat
Add the eggs and stir slowly
Take them off the heat while the egg is still glossy
Season off the heat
questions.explanation: Low heat from start to finish and taking them off early are what separate creamy from rubbery.
questions.explainWrong: Seasoning at the start makes the white release water and the eggs turn watery. And waiting for the finished look on the heat is always too late.

questions.prompt: A fried egg with firm white and soft yolk: which heat?
options: Medium-low, with a lid on at the end
High, so the white sets fast
Low from the start, never covered
High at first and then switched off
questions.correctAnswer: Medium-low, with a lid on at the end
questions.explanation: The lid sends heat back from above and finishes the white around the yolk, without cooking the yolk from below.
questions.explainWrong: On high heat the base goes lacy and tough before the white on top sets — and for a soft yolk it would have had to come out long before that.

lessons.title: When the salt goes in
lessons.description: The same pinch of salt does different things depending on when it lands.

preparationSteps.title: Salt early
preparationSteps.description: Draws water out. Good for onion and aubergine, bad for eggs.

preparationSteps.title: Salt at the end
preparationSteps.description: You taste more of it with less, because it stays on the surface.

preparationSteps.title: Reducing concentrates
preparationSteps.description: In a sauce that will reduce, the salt from the start tastes stronger at the end.

preparationSteps.title: Always taste
preparationSteps.description: Tasting before salting is the only way not to salt twice.

tips.title: Salted aubergine: 20 minutes
tips.text: Salt it, wait about 20 minutes, pat it dry with a cloth and only then into the pan.

questions.prompt: You're going to reduce a sauce for half an hour. When do you salt?
options: A little at the start and adjust at the end, once it's reduced
All at the start, to give it time to cook in
All at the end, salt doesn't need cooking
Halfway through, as a compromise
questions.correctAnswer: A little at the start and adjust at the end, once it's reduced
questions.explanation: The water leaves, the salt stays. What was right at the start is salty once the sauce is down to half.
questions.explainWrong: Salting it all at the start is the classic mistake with reduced sauces: the salt doesn't increase, the water disappears — and there's no taking salt back out of a sauce.

questions.prompt: You salted the aubergine and ten minutes later there's water on the board. Did it go wrong?
options: Yes, all the flavour went into that water
No, that's exactly what salt does there
questions.correctAnswer: No, that's exactly what salt does there
questions.explanation: Salting aubergine early pulls out the bitter water and leaves it firm. The water coming out is the goal, not an accident.
questions.explainWrong: The flavour didn't leave with the water: what came out was moisture that would have steamed the aubergine instead of frying it. Without that step, it soaks up oil and goes soggy.

questions.prompt: Put the seasoning of a soup that will cook for an hour in order.
correctOrder: A pinch with the vegetables, at the start
Let it cook without touching the salt
Taste it when it is ready
Adjust the salt off the heat
questions.explanation: A pinch at the start helps the vegetables give up flavour; the adjustment is always at the end, when the soup is at its final volume.
questions.explainWrong: Adjusting the salt halfway through is adjusting for a volume of water that's still going to change. Only at the end is the soup the soup.

questions.prompt: A steak: salt before or after searing?
options: Before, and right before it hits the pan
Only after, otherwise it loses its juices
Halfway through the sear
It makes no difference
questions.correctAnswer: Before, and right before it hits the pan
questions.explanation: Salted right then, the surface is still dry and sears well. Salted far in advance, the meat goes wet and won't brown.
questions.explainWrong: Salt afterwards sits on the surface and never reaches the inside. And the middle ground — salting half an hour before — is the worst of both: moisture on the surface, and still no time to penetrate.

lessons.title: The water has to taste of something
lessons.description: It's the one time you season something you're going to throw away.

preparationSteps.title: Plenty of water
preparationSteps.description: Pasta needs room to move, otherwise it sticks.

preparationSteps.title: Salt it properly
preparationSteps.description: A level tablespoon per litre. It should taste like seawater.

preparationSteps.title: Salt after it boils
preparationSteps.description: Before boiling, the salt takes longer to dissolve and can mark the base.

preparationSteps.title: No oil in the water
preparationSteps.description: It floats on top and prevents nothing. Stirring in the first minutes is what prevents it.

questions.prompt: How much salt per litre of water for pasta?
questions.explanation: About ten grams, a level tablespoon. It's the only seasoning the pasta gets on the inside.
questions.explainWrong: A pinch seasons nothing — the pasta comes out bland and no sauce fixes that afterwards. A hundred grams, on the other hand, is genuine seawater and inedible.

questions.prompt: What's oil in the pasta water for?
options: Nothing: it floats on top and makes the sauce slide off
It stops the pasta sticking
It flavours the pasta
It makes the water boil faster
questions.correctAnswer: Nothing: it floats on top and makes the sauce slide off
questions.explanation: Oil doesn't mix with water and never reaches the pasta. What stops pasta sticking is stirring in the first minute and having enough water.
questions.explainWrong: It's the most repeated piece of kitchen advice and one of the most useless: oil floats. Worse, it clings to the pasta as you drain it and makes the sauce slip instead of grip.

questions.prompt: Put cooking pasta in order.
correctOrder: Water on the heat, plenty of it
Wait for a proper boil
Add the salt
Add the pasta and stir for the first minute
Keep a mug of the water before draining
questions.explanation: The cooking water carries starch and salt: it's what binds the sauce to the pasta at the end.
questions.explainWrong: Dropping the pasta in before a proper boil makes the temperature fall and the pasta soften outside while it waits. And pouring everything down the sink throws away the sauce's best ingredient.

questions.prompt: This pasta is in a small pot, with the strands still sticking out above the water. Will it do?
options: Yes, it saves water and time
No, with little water the pasta sticks and cooks badly
questions.correctAnswer: No, with little water the pasta sticks and cooks badly
questions.explanation: Too little water cools too much when the pasta goes in and concentrates the starch. The result is stuck pasta with a pasty surface.
questions.explainWrong: The saving is real but small, and the cost is the whole dish. A big pot at a rolling boil is what keeps the pasta moving and cooking evenly.

questions.prompt: Why do you salt the water only after it boils?
options: The salt dissolves at once and doesn't mark the base of the pot
Salting beforehand stops the water ever boiling
To use less salt
Because cold salt damages the pot
questions.correctAnswer: The salt dissolves at once and doesn't mark the base of the pot
questions.explanation: In cold water the grains settle and can leave marks on the base of some pots. In boiling water they vanish instantly.
questions.explainWrong: Salt doesn't stop water boiling — it delays the boil almost imperceptibly, a matter of seconds. The reason is practical, not physical.

lessons.title: Two of water to one of rice
lessons.description: You don't taste rice while it cooks: you get it right beforehand and trust the ratio.

preparationSteps.title: Measure with the same cup
preparationSteps.description: What counts is the ratio, not the cup. One of rice, two of water.

preparationSteps.title: Toast the rice
preparationSteps.description: A minute in the oil before the water. The grains separate better.

preparationSteps.title: Boil, then drop it
preparationSteps.description: Bring it to the boil, drop to low and cover.

preparationSteps.title: Don't lift the lid
preparationSteps.description: Every peek lets out the steam that's cooking the rice on top.

questions.prompt: For one cup of long-grain rice, how many cups of water?
questions.explanation: Two. The rice absorbs all the water and the steam does the rest — which is why you don't drain it.
questions.explainWrong: With one cup the rice stays raw on top, and with four it swims and turns to mush. The ratio isn't a detail: it's the whole recipe.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't you lift the lid off rice halfway through cooking?
options: The steam that escapes is what's cooking the grains on top
The rice cools down and has to start again
Cold air gets in and the rice hardens
It makes no difference at all
questions.correctAnswer: The steam that escapes is what's cooking the grains on top
questions.explanation: Under the lid there are two cooks going on: water below and steam above. Lifting the lid ends the second one.
questions.explainWrong: It isn't the cold: it's the steam you lose. The rice on top keeps hard grains while the rice below overcooks, and none of that can be fixed later.

questions.prompt: Put loose rice in order.
correctOrder: Sweat the rice in the oil for a minute
Add double the water and the salt
Bring it to the boil
Drop to low and cover
Let it rest five minutes off the heat
questions.explanation: The final rest is part of the cooking: the moisture spreads out and the grains come apart.
questions.explainWrong: Serving the moment the water goes gives you rice that's wet at the bottom and dry on top. Five minutes covered, off the heat, is what evens out the whole pot.

questions.prompt: This rice still has water on the surface and the time is up. Do you serve it?
options: Yes, the water gets absorbed on the plate
No, cover it and give it a few more minutes on very low heat
questions.correctAnswer: No, cover it and give it a few more minutes on very low heat
questions.explanation: Water on the surface means there's still cooking or evaporating to do. A few more minutes covered sorts it without breaking the grains.
questions.explainWrong: On the plate the water doesn't disappear — it stays there, and the rice reaches the table soggy. The pot is still hot, and covered it fixes this in two or three minutes.

questions.prompt: What's toasting the rice in oil before the water for?
options: It coats the grain and helps it stay loose instead of sticky
It makes the rice cook faster
It's only for the taste of the oil
It stops the rice absorbing water
questions.correctAnswer: It coats the grain and helps it stay loose instead of sticky
questions.explanation: Fat around the grain slows the starch coming out, and starch is what makes grains cling to each other.
questions.explainWrong: It doesn't change the time or stop absorption — the rice drinks the water either way. What changes is the texture: loose instead of clumped.

lessons.title: Al dente is tasted, not read
lessons.description: The time on the packet is a suggestion from someone who knows neither your hob nor your sauce.

preparationSteps.title: Taste early
preparationSteps.description: Two minutes before the packet time, fish out a piece and bite it.

preparationSteps.title: Look for the white line
preparationSteps.description: Snap a piece: a white thread in the middle means al dente.

preparationSteps.title: Drain it early
preparationSteps.description: Pasta finishes cooking in the sauce, not in the colander.

preparationSteps.title: Into the sauce
preparationSteps.description: A minute in the pan with the sauce and a little of the cooking water.

questions.prompt: When do you drain pasta that's going into a pan of sauce?
options: A minute early: it finishes cooking in the sauce
Exactly at the packet time
A minute late, so it's soft
When there's no white line left at all
questions.correctAnswer: A minute early: it finishes cooking in the sauce
questions.explanation: In the sauce the pasta keeps cooking and takes on flavour. Drained at the exact point, it reaches the table overcooked.
questions.explainWrong: The packet time assumes the pasta goes straight to the plate. If it's still going through the pan, that extra minute happens twice.

questions.prompt: You snapped a spaghetti strand and there's a thin white thread in the centre. Is it al dente?
options: Yes, that's exactly the sign
No, white in the middle means raw pasta
questions.correctAnswer: Yes, that's exactly the sign
questions.explanation: The white thread is starch that hasn't hydrated yet. A thin thread is al dente; a thick, opaque core is raw.
questions.explainWrong: There's a difference between a thin thread and a thick white centre. The first is the point; the second is pasta that still needs a minute or two.

questions.prompt: How many minutes before the packet time should you first taste it?
questions.explanation: Two minutes before. You're still in time to fix it, and you can already tell where the pasta is heading.
questions.explainWrong: Tasting at the exact packet time is arriving too late to do anything. And tasting right at the start only tells you the pasta is raw, which you knew.

questions.prompt: Put bringing pasta and sauce together in order.
correctOrder: Taste the pasta two minutes before the time
Keep a mug of the cooking water
Drain it while the pasta is still al dente
Add it to the pan with the sauce
Add cooking water until the sauce coats it
questions.explanation: The starch in that water is what makes the sauce cling to the pasta instead of pooling at the bottom of the plate.
questions.explainWrong: Rinsing the pasta under cold water washes all that starch away and the sauce stops gripping. You only do that when the pasta is going into a cold salad.

questions.prompt: The pasta went past the point and turned soft. What can you do?
options: Nothing that brings it back: the starch has broken down
Rinse it in cold water and reheat it
Add more sauce to hide it
Put it back in the boiling water briefly
questions.correctAnswer: Nothing that brings it back: the starch has broken down
questions.explanation: Pasta's structure doesn't rebuild itself. That's why you taste early — the only possible fix happens beforehand.
questions.explainWrong: Cold water stops the cooking but doesn't give the texture back, and more sauce is still sauce on ruined pasta. This is a mistake you avoid, not one you fix.

lessons.title: Start with what takes longest
lessons.description: Cooking a whole dish is mostly deciding where to start.

preparationSteps.title: Read it all first
preparationSteps.description: The entire recipe before you switch anything on.

preparationSteps.title: Spot what takes longest
preparationSteps.description: Water coming to the boil and the oven heating start before everything else.

preparationSteps.title: Count backwards
preparationSteps.description: From the time you want to serve, work every step backwards.

preparationSteps.title: Slot in the quick jobs
preparationSteps.description: Anything that takes two minutes gets done while the rest cooks.

questions.prompt: Pasta with tomato sauce and a salad. What's the first move?
options: Put the water on, since it takes longest and doesn't need you
Cut the salad, it's quick
Start the sauce, it's the most important part
Wash up from breakfast
questions.correctAnswer: Put the water on, since it takes longest and doesn't need you
questions.explanation: Water boils by itself. Anything that works without you starts first, so your time is free for the rest.
questions.explainWrong: Cutting the salad first spends your ten useful minutes on something that takes two — and at the end you're still waiting for the water with the sauce going cold.

questions.prompt: Put the start of a pasta dinner in order.
correctOrder: Read the whole recipe
Put the water on the heat
Cut and prepare everything while the water heats
Make the sauce
Cook the pasta when the sauce is nearly done
questions.explanation: The pasta goes in last because it's the thing that waits worst. Everything else holds for a few minutes; cooked pasta doesn't.
questions.explainWrong: Cooking the pasta first, to "get it out of the way", leaves it sticking in the colander while the sauce is made. Pasta always goes in last.

questions.prompt: On this counter there are three pans on the heat at once and nothing chopped. Is that good organisation?
options: Yes, doing everything at once saves time
No, the chopping should have been done before the first pan went on
questions.correctAnswer: No, the chopping should have been done before the first pan went on
questions.explanation: With the heat on, the clock belongs to the hob. Chopping in a hurry with three pans running is how things burn.
questions.explainWrong: Doing everything at once isn't the same as doing things in parallel. What runs in parallel is what doesn't need you — chopping does.

questions.prompt: How long does a pot of water take to come to the boil on high heat?
questions.explanation: About ten minutes for a big pot. It's time you win back if the water is the first thing on the hob.
questions.explainWrong: A minute is what intuition says and it's never true with a full pot. It's precisely because it takes so long that this is the first step of any pasta dinner.

questions.prompt: Everything is ready except the steak, which takes four minutes. When do you cook it?
options: Last, with the rest already plated or covered
First, so I don't miss the doneness
Halfway, while the sauce reduces
Before everything, then reheat it
questions.correctAnswer: Last, with the rest already plated or covered
questions.explanation: Seared meat doesn't wait: it loses its juices and the crust softens. Whatever goes last is always what waits worst.
questions.explainWrong: Searing first and reheating is cooking the steak twice — and the second time ruins the first. The rest of the dish waits better than it does.

lessons.title: Seasoning goes in layers
lessons.description: A well-seasoned dish didn't take a lot of salt at the end: it took a little, several times.

preparationSteps.title: Season each stage
preparationSteps.description: The onion gets its pinch, the sauce gets its own, the plate gets the final adjustment.

preparationSteps.title: Always taste first
preparationSteps.description: Taste, then decide. Never salt blind.

preparationSteps.title: Acid wakes the rest up
preparationSteps.description: A dish that tastes flat sometimes doesn't need salt, it needs lemon.

preparationSteps.title: Finish on the plate
preparationSteps.description: Coarse salt and raw olive oil at the end come through far more.

tips.title: Taste several times
tips.text: In a half-hour dish, taste about four times: at every big change and at the end.

questions.prompt: One soffritto seasoned only at the end, another seasoned at every stage. What's the difference?
options: The layered one tastes seasoned all the way through, not just on the surface
None, the salt ends up spread out either way
The one seasoned at the end is saltier
The layered one takes less time
questions.correctAnswer: The layered one tastes seasoned all the way through, not just on the surface
questions.explanation: Salt needs time and heat to get into ingredients. Added at the end, it sits on the outside and reads as a spike instead of flavour.
questions.explainWrong: Salt doesn't redistribute itself in a finished dish. That's why two dishes with the same amount of salt can taste completely different.

questions.prompt: The sauce has enough salt but still tastes flat. What do you try first?
options: A few drops of lemon or vinegar
More salt, until it tastes of something
More time on the heat
More olive oil
questions.correctAnswer: A few drops of lemon or vinegar
questions.explanation: Acid lifts what's already there. A "flat" dish is often short on acidity, not on salt.
questions.explainWrong: Adding more salt to a sauce that already has enough gives you a salty sauce that's still flat — and from there there's no way back.

questions.prompt: Put the seasoning of a tomato sauce in order, from start to finish.
correctOrder: A pinch of salt on the onion as it sweats
A pinch on the tomato, as it goes in
Let it reduce without touching the salt
Taste at the end
Adjust with salt and a touch of acid
questions.explanation: Each pinch seasons what's in the pan at that moment. The final adjustment is about the whole thing, at its final volume.
questions.explainWrong: A single dose of salt at the start doesn't survive the reduction — it ends up salty. And a single dose at the end never gets into the ingredients.

questions.prompt: This steak got coarse salt scattered over it after it came off the heat. Does that make sense?
options: Yes, raw seasoning at the end comes through far more
No, everything should have been seasoned on the heat
questions.correctAnswer: Yes, raw seasoning at the end comes through far more
questions.explanation: Whole crystals of coarse salt that never dissolved in the pan give bursts of seasoning and a crunch that salt stirred in earlier can't.
questions.explainWrong: The two don't compete: seasoning on the heat builds the base, raw seasoning is the finish. A dish with only one of them always stops halfway.

lessons.title: The plate is part of serving
lessons.description: The last minute decides whether it looks like food made by someone who cared.

preparationSteps.title: Warm plates
preparationSteps.description: Hot food on a cold plate goes cold before the second forkful.

preparationSteps.title: Height, not spread
preparationSteps.description: Gather it in the centre instead of covering the whole plate.

preparationSteps.title: Wipe the rim
preparationSteps.description: A cloth around the edge changes everything and costs three seconds.

preparationSteps.title: Serve straight away
preparationSteps.description: Plating is the last step, not a moment for a long photo shoot.

tips.title: Leave the rim clean
tips.text: About 2 cm free around the food makes the plate look composed instead of crowded.

tips.title: Plating is quick
tips.text: With plates and spoons to hand, two plates take under a minute — the food is going cold.

questions.prompt: Why do you warm the plates?
options: A cold plate steals the food's heat in seconds
So the food doesn't slide
It's just restaurant presentation
It makes the sauce thicker
questions.correctAnswer: A cold plate steals the food's heat in seconds
questions.explanation: Cold ceramic absorbs the heat of whatever you put on it. A warm plate keeps food hot for as long as it takes to eat.
questions.explainWrong: It isn't a restaurant luxury: it's the difference between a hot steak and a lukewarm one by the third forkful. Hot tap water in the plate for a minute is enough.

questions.prompt: This plate has food spread to the rim and splashes of sauce over the edge. Do you serve it like that?
options: Yes, it tastes the same
No, gather it to the centre and wipe the rim with a cloth
questions.correctAnswer: No, gather it to the centre and wipe the rim with a cloth
questions.explanation: A clean rim is the frame. It costs three seconds and it's the difference between food served and food dumped.
questions.explainWrong: It does taste the same — but people eat with their eyes first, and after thirty minutes of work it's worth not losing the dish on the last move.

questions.prompt: Put plating in order.
correctOrder: Warm the plates
Put the base down, in the centre
Put what the dish is about on top
Sauce and raw seasoning
Wipe the rims and serve straight away
questions.explanation: Bottom up, always finishing with what you don't want cooked any further: the fresh sauce and the raw olive oil.
questions.explainWrong: Wiping the rim before adding the sauce means wiping twice. And raw seasoning put on first gets buried, which is the same as not adding it.
